name: Automate what you do twice by hand
statement: The second time a manual step is repeated, build the tool, document it in the repository's agent notes and log, and use cheap compute (CI) where it can. The ship script, the gate, the splitter, the scans and the timing report each began as a step done by hand twice.

name: Release in batches, not on every merge
statement: A release per merge costs minutes of waiting and gives users a new version every few minutes, while proving little that CI does not. Release when about ten changes wait, or the oldest has waited a week, or a change touches how releases are *published* (the one thing only a release proves), or on request. Make the policy a small tested function.

name: One branch, one merged pull request per iteration
statement: Each iteration is a branch from the current main, a pull request whose body says what and why and shows the evidence, and a squash merge with a conventional title. History reads as the story of the work, and nothing depends on a conversation.

name: Check the property, not the symptom
statement: A compile, a green build or a passing test is not the check that a change did what you meant. Check the property itself: that no string literal changed under a rename, that the output is byte-identical, that the real program says what you think it says. Almost every surprise in this project was a symptom taken for the property.

name: The levers that paid
statement: A prebuilt tool instead of compiling it; a timeout on every job; the cache saved only from main; narrower triggers so a documents-only change skips the heavy jobs; no incremental builds or full debug info in CI; retries on the network. A policy swap (here, the audit's rules) was proven locally against a known-bad case before it replaced the old one.

name: Decide, following the canon and the project's interest
statement: An agent given a principle decides, and says what it decided and why, instead of handing the choice back. It asks only when the answer needs something it cannot know, and it checks between iterations that each action still serves the purpose and is not busy work.

name: Documents are checked against the code
statement: A document that names a path is checked to name a real one; a code example in a document is compared with the source; a page about how close the code is to the ideal says where it is not close. A guess written as fact is corrected in writing when it turns out wrong, and so is an invented date.

name: A fast local gate; CI for the rest
statement: One command runs what must pass before shipping (format, lint, docs, links, licences, tests), writes each step's log to a file and prints one line per step. CI runs the heavy matrix. The gate is for reproducing a failure and for catching mistakes early, not a substitute for the pull request.

name: Findability as a test
statement: Generate an outline from every module's first sentence, then ask it real questions in a test ("where is it said which kind of disk we work with?") and fail if the answer is not near the top. A cold read, turned into something that runs on every change. If a description is vague, or a thing is in the wrong place, it shows here first.

name: Generalise a tool with a parity test
statement: When a script built for one project is made general, run the general one and the original on the original's own project and compare the results. If they differ, form a hypothesis and test it with a controlled experiment (give the new one the old one's exact rule and see whether the results then match) until every difference is explained and deliberate. A generalisation that is 'about the same' has changed something nobody chose.

name: Pin the real output
statement: Record the exact text of the program's commands on a real fixture, and fail CI when it differs. A change to wording then shows as the few lines that moved, reviewed as such. Re-record only after reading the diff: a recording of empty output looks as clean as a good one until you read it.

name: Guards are tests that read the source
statement: Architecture rules are ordinary tests that read the source tree (or its parsed form) and fail naming the file and line. A rule that lives only in a document is a wish; a rule that fails the build is a property of the project.

name: Look at what people will see
statement: A check that a page answers, or that every link on it resolves, cannot see that it looks wrong. Look at it the way a reader will: a screenshot of the real page in a real browser, of the live site and not only of a local build. Three defects of this playbook's own site (literals not styled as code, a table of contents drawn like the navigation bar, headings drawn as links) were visible only that way.

name: Measure before you claim
statement: Say how long, how many, how big, before and after, with the samples, and say when the samples overlap. A claim chosen from the best runs is not a measurement. When you find you overclaimed, retract it in writing, where the claim was made.

name: Measure the CI before optimising it
statement: Collect wall time, job-minutes and the slowest jobs and steps over several runs, then change the critical path. The biggest win here was one step, a security audit that compiled its own tool for three minutes. Reject, with reasons, what the measurement does not support.

name: Names explain the program
statement: Names of files, folders, actions and states say what the thing is for, in plain words. Folders are named for what the program is *for*, not for how it is built (`going_back/`, not `adapters/`). A part's first sentence says what it is for without a pattern word like adapter or port.

name: Judge CI by the newest run of each check
statement: Reruns and flakes leave old failures in the history. Judge a commit by the newest run of each check name, count skipped as passing, and rerun a job the runner itself failed to start. A release is the commit titled as one, not the merge before it.

name: A fact, a word or a rule lives in one place
statement: A sentence a person reads, a plural, a rule about disks, a way of counting: written once, in the layer that owns it, and used everywhere. Every copy is a place it can come out differently. Guards forbid the copy, and a helper makes the one place cheap to use.

name: Report in plain words, at the big picture
statement: Say what changed, how much closer it is to the ideal, what went wrong, and what is next, in language a person who does not read the code can follow. Technical detail belongs in the log and the pull request. Own mistakes briefly and say what they taught.

name: Prove every guard bites
statement: A guard that has only ever passed is unproven. Break the thing it guards on purpose, in a clean file, confirm it fails with a useful message, then restore the file *exactly* (and compare). Two checks can pass together for the wrong reason, for example a link and its target both wrong in the same way, so test the rule against the outside truth too.

name: Published identities are not renamed for a word
statement: A key in a JSON output, a contract's identity, a stored word in a journal: other programs and older files read them. Give people a plain word beside the stored one, test both, and leave the stored one alone, with the reason written down.

name: Remove a race by construction
statement: A rare failure is not disproved by many clean runs on a fast machine. Find the shared resource, put every use behind one lock, and show with a stress test that the original fails and the fixed version does not.

name: Debts are data and only shrink
statement: A rule that cannot be met today is recorded as a number per file in a data file. The test fails if any number grows, and insists the file record any decrease. Progress cannot silently slip back, and what remains is a list anyone can read.

name: A stateless, resumable shipper
statement: One script pushes, opens the pull request, waits for checks, merges and verifies. It keeps no state of its own, reading GitHub every time, and it stops itself before the tool's time limit with a code that means *run me again*. Any session can continue what another began.

name: Retire a word with a guard
statement: When a word is wrong (here, *config* for an area), rename its uses with a lexer-based tool that follows string interpolation and verifies no literal changed, then add a guard that the word is not an identifier outside the adapter that owns it.

name: Say what to do next, once
statement: Every situation where nothing is there, or something failed, says what to do about it, in the layer that owns the words, so every surface (command line, window) is equally helpful and none repeats it differently.

name: Search by shape, and read all of the results
statement: To find a smell, search by its *shape* (every bare bool in a pair, every `if n == 1`), not by the instance you noticed. Read the whole result: a search cut off after ten lines once hid the one script that pinned a change, and CI found it.

name: Seeded cold reads
statement: Pick modules at random with a seed (so the read is reproducible), read them as a stranger, and write down where you stumbled. It finds what no guard measures: a rule copied by hand, a stale word, a distinction the code makes and never names. It stops paying when a seed returns modules you have already read; that is the signal to read differently.

name: Each layer is a small language
statement: A layer offers a vocabulary (types, verbs, nouns) and the layer above is written in it. A command reads as a story of those words: look, ask, begin, do, end, show. The reader meets the story first and the mechanism only when they ask.

name: State and plans live in the repository
statement: An agent's memory is not the project's memory. The plan (backlog), the decisions (log), the rules (agent notes) and the documentation of the tools are files in the repository, so no session starts over and any agent can continue where another stopped.

name: The stranger test
statement: Someone who has never seen the code should be able to say what a part is for from its first line, and be right. It is the measure of clarity, and the only one that cannot be gamed by moving code around.

name: Tools that rewrite code verify themselves
statement: A splitter, a renamer or a formatter that edits many files checks its own work: every comment survives, no string literal changed, nothing is written unless everything matches. A regex rename once changed a JSON key and a fake tool's output; a lexer-based one that verifies the strings changed none.

name: Every layer is the top of the layers beneath it
statement: Read from the top, each part says what it is *for*, in the words a person uses; each step down says *how*, using only the words of the layer beneath it. You can stop at any level and still understand the program, and you never have to hold all of it in your head. This is the one idea the rest of the playbook serves.

name: Two faces: what it is for, and a body in the words beneath
statement: Every part has an upward face (its purpose, and the words it offers) and a downward face (a body written only in the words of the layers below). A part that cannot be described that way is doing two jobs, and is split.

name: Use the program as a newcomer would
statement: Run the real program on a real disk, from first use to going back, and read every word it says; drive a terminal UI through a pseudo-terminal and print its screens. Reading code finds what is wrong with code; only using the program finds what is wrong with what it *says*.

name: Chainability
summary: One project's data can feed another's - device tests into a grand project's path, a tool's releases into a lab's - each row carrying where it came from.
why: An ecosystem, not a heap: data flows along the real relations between projects.

name: Data made by work
summary: A project's data is produced by its development and its functioning - commits, builds, tests, releases, measurements - as a principle and by tools, never kept by hand.
why: Hand-kept data goes stale and lies; data made by work is as true as the work.

name: tad, the format
summary: Text as data - tables as JSON lines with a schema, a canonical form and verification - is the format ocoeco speaks.
why: Readable by people, diffable by git, checkable by machines.

name: The board
summary: A project's live work - ongoing, waiting, planned - kept as data and shown in the picture next to its path.
why: What is being done now, next to where it leads.

name: The conveyor
summary: A forkable lab that holds everything a person or an agent needs to bring a goal about - for phones: tools, procedures, safety rules, principles; projects made from it carry the mark.
why: Anyone can join with no setup and contribute back; every project fits the picture by construction.

name: Discovery, hexagonal
summary: Finding projects is a port; each platform is an outlet - GitHub first, others (GitLab, Open Hub) later without touching the core.
why: The observatory is not tied to one platform.

name: A grand project's family
summary: The grand project's repository and every project whose parent is its owner or itself.
why: Each grand project's views show its own projects' data, and only theirs.

name: Grand project
summary: A marked project of kind picture: a large aim with its own tab, views and family of projects (Linux Phones is the first).
why: The observatory's navigation follows the commons' great aims, not any one of their parts.

name: The harvest
summary: On a schedule, the observatory reads every marked project's shared tables, tags each row with its project and merges them; problems are shown, not lost.
why: The picture keeps itself current.

name: Lens
summary: A repository of its own (kind lens) that declares a family of projects and the views that show it - from a small shared vocabulary (path, matrix, families, runs, backlog, log, ideas, heartbeat, cards). The observatory discovers lenses and renders each with the same engine; curated lenses take its navigation, every other is listed among the discovered.
why: Views hard-coded in the observatory made it a gatekeeper; lenses let anyone make a grand view of their own family of projects, built exactly as the observatory's own.

name: The mark
summary: oco.toml at a repository's root plus the oco-project topic (and oco-kind-<kind>): which project it is, its kind, its parent, the tables it shares.
why: A repository becomes a piece of the picture by itself; discovery is one search of GitHub's index.

name: Milestone
summary: A stop on a project's path, on one horizon, with criteria tied to measured data (feature statuses, tests, health); it fills by itself as evidence arrives, never by hand.
why: Progress that cannot be argued with: each step says what proves it.

name: The observatory
summary: A meta structure, tied to no project: one living picture of every project of the open commons, built from the projects' own data.
why: So the commons can be seen whole, and every project's place in it, without anyone keeping the picture by hand.

name: The observer
summary: Half-manual tests ask an observer - a person today, a rig of cameras and servos later - with nothing else changing.
why: Tests that need eyes and hands still run as a conveyor.

name: ocoeco
summary: The observatory's information ecosystem and its backbone - both a principle (data is produced by projects as they are made and as they work, never by hand) and a tool (formats and protocols, gatherers, chaining, propagation), in the repository ocoeco.
why: It is the working system of the whole picture; naming it makes it something to design and tend.

name: The path
summary: A project's visit card: a line through its three horizons, its milestones as stops, filled to where the evidence shows - and unknown shown as unknown.
why: One view that says where a project is and what is next, beautifully, for every project the same way.

name: The readiness ladder
summary: Under the horizons, a project's maturity on the established Technology Readiness Levels (concept to proven in operation), so projects of any kind compare on one scale.
why: An established, project-agnostic scale, rather than one invented here.

name: Shared parts as rhizcuts
summary: tad, the mark and the conveyor's tools travel as rhizoid modules: owned, patchable git forks rather than template copies or subtrees.
why: Transparent dependencies that click in like puzzle pieces and send fixes back.

name: tad, the heart
summary: tad - text as data - is the living heart and blood of oco-eco: the formats every project's data is kept in, the gatherers that fill them, the views that show them; supplied in every repository as a rhizcut.
why: Everything the observatory shows flows through tad.

name: Text as data (tad)
summary: Everything a project knows - plans, decisions, concepts, progress, measurements - is kept as tad data in its own repository, and rendered from there.
why: Nothing important lives only in a person's or an agent's memory; anyone can pick up where others left off.

name: Three horizons
summary: Every project is measured against three: working (it does its job end to end), perfection (complete and polished - as good as it should be), ongoing perfection (it stays so: healthy, free of regressions, upstreamed, maintained).
why: One percentage hides where a project stands; three honest horizons show how close it is to working, to perfect, and to staying perfect.

name: Unknown is not failure
summary: What has not been measured is shown as not known yet - never counted as missing or broken.
why: Honest pictures: a gap in knowledge is work to do, not a verdict.
